newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. Dec personal income seen up solidly.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. Dec personal income seen up solidly.

text.p: Increases in earnings, the workweek and jobs augur a solid gain in U.S. personal income in December, said economists, but a mild pick-up in spending for services and lower vehicle sales suggest personal consumption rose modestly.
Preliminary estimates show December personal income up about 0.7 percent, and spending increasing around 0.5 percent.
The Commerce Department is scheduled to release the data on Monday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. In November, both personal income and consumption climbed 0.5 percent.
Economists looked primarily to the December employment report to extrapolate their personal income forecasts.

"It's a fairly straightforward analysis that wage and salary growth was probably quite good given the rise in earnings and the rise in employment and the rise in the work week," said Sally Kleinman, a vice president and senior domestic economist at Chase Securities Inc.
In the final month of 1996, the economy generated 262,000 non-farm payroll jobs, hourly earnings rose to $12.05 from $11.99 in November and average weekly hours climbed to 34.8 from 34.5 in November.
Kleinman speculated that the increase in December personal income could be even larger than 0.7 percent.
Yet Kleinman said she tempered the forecasted 0.7 percent gain in personal income because large surges in the employment indicators do not necessarily translate one for one into income growth.

On the other side of the ledger, economists scrutinized spending on products such as apparel and autos, and for services such as insurance, utilities and dry cleaning to determine the strength of consumption in December.
"December spending looks to be fairly moderate by all indications from the chain store sales figures that we've seen," said Kim Rupert, a senior economist at MMS International Inc.
Kleinman noted that the number of cars and trucks sold in December did decline. "So, there's probably some weakness there," she added.
By contrast, Kleinman said, "I'm presuming the services are up which ... gives you positive consumption rather than a flatter looking number."
Although economists expect a solid rise in personal income in December, some pointed out that income growth on a yearly basis has slowed.
William Griggs, a managing director at Griggs and Santow Inc, noted that personal income grew 6.3 percent from December 1994 to December 1995, but increased only 5.3 percent through November 1996.
Griggs said income is growing more slowly and encouraging consumers to be sure to continue to spend at a reasonable pace and not get overburdened.
